strengths: Well-motivated conceptual framework: Adapting speculative decoding to autoregressive vision models by exploiting natural 2D visual priors—specifically multi-scale resolution hierarchies and 2D spatial locality—addresses fundamental limitations of applying 1D text-based speculative decoding to images.

Innovative local verification and expansion mechanism: Replacing the traditional 1D raster-scan cascade rejection with a 2D neighborhood expansion rule ($R_X$) effectively mitigates error propagation while avoiding the excessive resampling typical of standard speculative decoding.

Extensive and informative ablation studies: The paper clearly isolates the contributions of each design choice, including up/down-sampler loss formulations (MSE + LPIPS + PatchGAN vs. latent cross-entropy), the impact of probability pooling, and the local neighborhood expansion radius.

Thorough latency and algorithmic analysis: The manuscript and supplementary material provide detailed breakdowns of time spent across drafting, up/down-sampling, verification, and resampling, along with comprehensive qualitative sweeps across acceptance thresholds.
weaknesses: Evaluation restricted to a single model architecture: All experimental evaluations are conducted strictly on Tar-1.5B (using AR-DTok / LlamaGen backbone). Validating the approach across other prominent visual AR models (e.g., standalone LlamaGen, Janus/Janus-Pro, or Lumina-mGPT) would significantly strengthen the claims of general applicability.

Modest speedups relative to orthogonal non-speculative approaches: While MuLo-SD outperforms prior speculative decoders (EAGLE-2, LANTERN), it achieves 1.22x (at 512p) and 1.68x (at 1024p), whereas training-free parallel decoding (ZipAR) achieves 1.88x and 3.65x with negligible metric degradation. While orthogonal, the practical utility of speculative decoding over spatial parallel decoding remains somewhat in question unless a hybrid integration is empirically demonstrated.

End-to-end pipeline latency perspective: In unified MLLMs like Tar, the text/condition generation phase alone takes ~17 seconds, which is excluded from the speedup calculation. In an end-to-end system context, a 1.68x speedup on AR-DTok alone yields a noticeably smaller total wall-clock speedup for the complete pipeline.

Training overhead and pipeline complexity: Unlike standard speculative decoding that relies on lightweight drafting heads or off-the-shelf smaller models, MuLo-SD introduces learned multi-stage convolutional up- and down-samplers trained with multi-component objectives (MSE, LPIPS, GAN, commitment loss) for hundreds of thousands of steps, increasing system complexity.

strengths: Novel integration of multi-scale representation into speculative decoding: Combining a low-resolution autoregressive drafter with learned up/down-samplers specifically tailored for image generation provides a fresh perspective on accelerating visual autoregressive models.

Locality-aware verification and expansion: The proposed local rejection and neighborhood expansion mechanism smartly exploits the 2D spatial inductive bias of visual data, effectively mitigating the severe cascade rejection issue typical of 1D raster-scan speculative decoding.

Comprehensive ablation studies: The paper provides informative ablations dissecting key architectural choices, including the up/down-sampler loss formulations (MSE, LPIPS, GAN), the neighborhood expansion radius, and the impact of probability pooling.
Clarity and presentation: The manuscript is well-structured, featuring clear algorithmic descriptions (Algorithm 1) and helpful schematic overviews (Figure 2 and Figure 6).
weaknesses: Limited evaluation breadth across architectures: Experiments are conducted exclusively on a single base model family, Tar-1.5B (using AR-DTok/LlamaGen 600M). To establish generalizability across the visual AR domain, evaluation on other popular visual AR frameworks (e.g., native LlamaGen, Janus/Janus-Pro, or Lumina-mGPT) is necessary.

Unfavorable speedup-to-complexity trade-off compared to existing alternatives: MuLo-SD achieves modest speedups (1.22x at 512p and 1.68x at 1024p). Meanwhile, existing training-free parallel decoding methods like ZipAR achieve significantly higher speedups (1.88x at 512p and 3.65x at 1024p) on the exact same model with negligible quality loss. Although parallel decoding is orthogonal, requiring a multi-stage training pipeline (training causal up/down-samplers with GAN objectives for 300k total steps) for a 1.68x speedup limits the practical appeal.

Loss of theoretical sampling guarantees and distributional shifts: Standard speculative decoding guarantees exact sampling from the target distribution, and vision adaptations like LANTERN maintain bounded Total Variation Distance (TVD). In MuLo-SD, verification relies on a heuristic acceptance threshold (Eq. 5) paired with local neighborhood re-sampling and cyclic downsampling Dr(x). This creates compounding approximations whose effect on target distribution divergence is not theoretically characterized, as reflected in degraded FID scores at higher acceleration factors (Figure 8).

Dependency on multi-resolution pretrained checkpoints: The drafter model relies on having an existing, identical-architecture model pretrained at a lower resolution (AR-DTok @ 256p). Many modern generative AR setups are trained only at their final target token resolution, which restricts out-of-the-box applicability.

Drafter latency bottleneck at lower resolutions: Because the drafter model has identical parameter scale to the target model, its latency remains constant regardless of the acceptance rate. As acknowledged in Section 14 (Figure 7), this severely caps the acceleration potential for medium resolutions (512p).

strengths: The core idea of combining multi-scale drafting with spatially local verification is well-motivated for autoregressive visual generation, effectively exploiting spatial coherence and multi-resolution inductive biases.

The local rejection and expansion mechanism elegantly addresses a key limitation of standard speculative decoding in 2D image synthesis, preventing a single failure in raster-scan order from invalidating the rest of the draft sequence.
The paper includes comprehensive experimental validation with wall-clock latency measurements on A100 GPUs, standard alignment benchmarks (GenEval, DPG-Bench), and perceptual metrics (FID, HPSv2).

Detailed ablation studies provide valuable insights into architectural and training choices, specifically highlighting the importance of pixel-space adversarial/perceptual losses for the upsampler, probability pooling, and expansion radius.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is restricted to a single foundation model (Tar-1.5B). Evaluating across other popular autoregressive frameworks (such as LlamaGen or Janus) would better demonstrate generalizability.

The practical utility is somewhat challenged by non-speculative parallel decoding baselines such as ZipAR, which achieves significantly higher speedups (1.88× at 512p and 3.65× at 1024p) training-free and with negligible metric drops, whereas combining ZipAR with MuLo-SD is only discussed as future work.

The method requires training specialized row-causal up- and down-samplers using a multi-component VQ-GAN objective (requiring substantial training time on 4× A100 GPUs), which increases engineering complexity compared to training-free or lighter drafting approaches.

Perceptual quality exhibits noticeable degradation as speedups increase; specifically, FID worsens from 32.4 to 32.8 at 1024p (and degrades sharply at more aggressive thresholds in Fig. 8), whereas LANTERN achieved a lower FID.

strengths: Well-motivated concept: Adapting speculative decoding to the 2D spatial nature of visual autoregressive generation by combining multi-scale drafting (low-resolution draft with upsampling) and localized verification is intuitive and conceptually sound.

Spatial rejection and island-based resampling: The introduction of local neighborhood expansion around rejected tokens and grouping rejected positions into connected components ('rejection islands') for concurrent resampling effectively leverages the spatial locality of image representations.

Comprehensive ablation studies: The paper systematically evaluates essential design choices, including latent vs. pixel-space upsampling, probability pooling, raster-scan vs. local rejection/expansion, and the neighborhood expansion radius.

Extensive supplementary material: Provides clear algorithm pseudocode, detailed step-by-step latency breakdowns, qualitative progression sweeps over the acceptance threshold, and architectural specifics.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on ZipAR for acceleration: A critical limitation is that the standalone multi-scale speculative decoding without parallel decoding achieves modest speedups (around 1.7x–2.2x at 1024p as shown in the Figure 7 latency breakdown), which is substantially slower than the training-free baseline ZipAR alone (3.65x speedup at 1024p). Most of the final headline speedup (e.g., 3.90x / 5.33x) is driven by embedding ZipAR into both the draft stage and the island resampling stage. In fact, on 512p, MULO-SD achieves 1.94x–2.03x, which is only marginally higher than ZipAR alone (1.88x), while introducing significant algorithmic complexity.

Pareto dominance concerns: As acknowledged in the supplementary text (Section 8) and visible in Figure 8, ZipAR dominates or matches MULO-SD across multiple quality vs. latency operating points without requiring draft models, upsamplers, or secondary caches.

Underperformance on LlamaGen: When tested on the standard LlamaGen benchmark at 512p, MULO-SD achieves 1.40x speedup, lagging behind both LANTERN (1.59x) and ZipAR (1.88x), indicating that the framework's effectiveness depends heavily on specific pre-trained multi-resolution checkpoints (like Tar) rather than general visual AR models.

Substantial memory and cache footprint: Maintaining two separate full autoregressive models (e.g., 256p drafter and 1024p verifier) requires storing two independent sets of model parameters and active KV-caches, imposing severe GPU memory overhead compared to self-speculative or single-model parallel decoding techniques.

Loss of theoretical guarantees: Unlike standard speculative decoding (which guarantees exact sampling from the target distribution) or LANTERN (which formally bounds total variation distance), MULO-SD relies on a heuristic acceptance threshold combined with local neighborhood expansion, departing from rigorous distributional guarantees.

strengths: The core idea of combining multi-scale drafting with 2D spatial locality verification is well-motivated for autoregressive visual generation, where raster-scan 1D order in standard speculative decoding fails to capture spatial context and token ambiguity.

The paper introduces practical and effective components, such as local neighborhood expansion around rejected tokens and island-wise parallel resampling, which directly address the serial verification bottlenecks.

Empirical acceleration is impressive at high resolutions, achieving up to 5.33x speedup on Tar-7B at 1024p while largely preserving semantic alignment (GenEval and DPG-Bench scores) compared to previous speculative baselines like LANTERN and EAGLE-2.
Comprehensive experimental analysis and ablations, including latency breakdowns across stages, comparison between latent and pixel-space upsamplers, and analyses of expansion radii.
weaknesses: Lack of theoretical distributional guarantees: Unlike standard speculative decoding which guarantees sampling from the exact target distribution, MULO-SD relies on a heuristic acceptance threshold and localized island resampling. Unlike LANTERN, there is no formal bound on the total variation distance for the entire generated sequence.

Performance on standard baselines at 512p (e.g., LlamaGen-XL) is less compelling: MULO-SD achieves a 1.40x speedup, lagging behind both standalone ZipAR (1.88x) and LANTERN (1.59x). The substantial gains primarily emerge at 1024p or when integrated with parallel decoding.

Memory footprint and hardware overhead are not quantified: Operating both a low-resolution drafter and a high-resolution verifier simultaneously requires maintaining two distinct KV-caches and model weights in VRAM, which could be a bottleneck on memory-constrained devices.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely challenge: autoregressive image generation suffers from high inference latency, and adapting speculative decoding to 2D image token generation is non-trivial due to flat token distributions and quadratic sequence growth.

Well-motivated integration of multi-scale hierarchy and 2D spatial locality: using a low-resolution AR model as a drafter combined with local neighborhood rejection expansion (and island-wise parallel resampling) effectively exploits the spatial inductive biases of visual autoregressive models.

Strong acceleration at high resolutions: achieving up to 5.33x speedup on Tar-7B at 1024p with minimal degradation in GenEval and DPG-Bench scores significantly outperforms previous image speculative decoding baselines such as LANTERN and EAGLE-2.

Comprehensive experimental analysis and ablations: the paper evaluates across multiple backbones (Tar-1.5B, Tar-7B, LlamaGen), compares learned vs. training-free upsamplers, ablates neighborhood expansion radii and probability pooling, and provides an insightful component-wise latency breakdown.
weaknesses: Heuristic nature of local rejection and causal dependency violation: unlike exact speculative decoding or LANTERN (which bounds total variation distance), MULO-SD replaces rejected tokens locally while retaining subsequent raster-scan tokens that were causally conditioned on the discarded draft tokens. The paper relies on empirical spatial locality heuristics without formal bounds or error propagation analysis.

Heavy reliance on ZipAR for practical speedups: on 512p generation, MULO-SD yields only marginal speedup over pure ZipAR (e.g., 1.94x vs. 1.88x on Tar-1.5B, and 1.40x vs. 1.88x on LlamaGen-XL, where MULO-SD is noticeably slower). The clear advantage over parallel decoding baselines only manifests at 1024p resolution.

High memory footprint and operational complexity: MULO-SD requires hosting two separate model checkpoints (drafter and verifier) with independent KV-caches simultaneously. Furthermore, the default training-free pixel upsampler requires decoding draft tokens to pixel space, executing an external super-resolution network, and re-encoding back to discrete tokens, introducing significant memory overhead and multi-stage pipeline complexity.

Trade-off in perceptual metrics: as noted in the supplementary material and Figure 8, FID degrades noticeably when sweeping the acceptance threshold to attain higher acceleration rates, showing that the relaxed multi-scale acceptance can negatively affect fine-grained visual distribution fidelity.
